candidates.title: Leap years aren't every four years
candidates.opening_promise: Leap years aren't every four years.

thumbnail.concept: a February page with day 29 crossed out

candidates.description: A century year is a leap year only if it divides by 400: 2000 was, 1900 was not, and 2100 will not be. The rule keeps the calendar in step with the seasons.
candidates.rationale: flips the rule everyone learned, exactly as the video opens

candidates.title: Why 1900 had no leap day
candidates.opening_promise: 1900 had no leap day, but 2000 did.

thumbnail.concept: one big badge with the divide-by-400 rule

candidates.description: Century years are leap years only if they divide by 400. That is why 2000 had a leap day, 1900 did not, and 2100 will not.
candidates.rationale: a concrete date that breaks the rule

candidates.title: In 1582, ten days were dropped
candidates.opening_promise: Too many leap years: by 1582, ten days had to go.

thumbnail.concept: an October page with a block of days struck out

candidates.description: By the 1500s the old calendar had drifted about 10 days, so in 1582 Thursday 4 October was followed by Friday 15 October. The century rule stops it drifting again.
candidates.rationale: the strange historical moment behind the rule

candidates.title: Why century years skip leap day
candidates.opening_promise: A leap day every four years overshoots the seasons.

thumbnail.concept: one big quarter-day clock under the number 365.25

candidates.description: A leap day every 4 years makes the average year 365.25 days, a little longer than the seasons. Skipping three century leap days every 400 years fixes it.
candidates.rationale: explains the arithmetic behind the rule
